_note: Batch 4 — concepts and technique. 48 answers. These are what a producer reads once and uses for years, so they explain the mechanism rather than giving a recipe. Where a number comes from a published standard it is named; where it is convention, it says so.

questions.q: How much headroom should I leave before mastering?
aliases: how loud should my mix be
questions.short: Peak around −6 dBFS and average around −18. The exact number matters less than not clipping.
steps: Aim for peaks at −6 dBFS and an average around −18 dBFS on the master.
Leave the mix bus limiter off, or bounce a second version without it.
Check for inter-sample peaks with a true-peak meter, not a sample-peak one.
If you mixed into a limiter, bounce both versions and say which is which.
questions.why: Digital headroom costs nothing, and a mastering engineer needs somewhere to work. The old rule of −6 dBFS comes from analogue converters with real headroom limits; in a 32-bit float session the number is a habit rather than a constraint, but it still protects you from inter-sample peaks that only appear after encoding.
questions.watch: Turning the master fader down at the end does not undo clipping that already happened inside a plugin.

questions.q: Should I mix into a limiter?
aliases: limiter on the master while mixing
questions.short: Yes, if you bounce without it. Mixing into one and sending that file is the mistake.
steps: Put a limiter on the master so you hear roughly the final loudness while deciding balance.
Keep it gentle — 2–3 dB, not 8 — or you are mixing a squashed version of your mix.
Bounce the delivery file with it bypassed.
Check the mix with it off every half hour; if it falls apart, the limiter is hiding a problem.
questions.why: Balance decisions change with loudness, so mixing quiet and mastering loud produces a mix that was balanced for the wrong playback level. The danger is not the limiter, it is forgetting it is there and letting it fix something the balance should have.
questions.watch: If you need more than 3 dB of limiting to make the mix feel right, the mix is the problem.

questions.q: What does clipping actually sound like?
questions.short: A hard crackle on transients and a flattening of everything else. On drums it can be useful.
steps: Listen for a crackle on the loudest transients, most audible on snares and vocal consonants.
Solo the suspect channel and watch the meter as well as listening.
On drums, 2–3 dB of deliberate soft clipping is a tool, not a fault.
On sustained sources — vocals, bass, pads — any clipping is audible and unwanted.
questions.why: Clipping flattens the top of a waveform, generating odd harmonics. On a transient that lasts two milliseconds the harmonics read as attack; on a sustained note they read as distortion, which is why the same process is a mixing technique on a kick and a fault on a voice.
questions.watch: Inter-sample peaks can clip after encoding even when your meter never showed red. Use a true-peak meter.

questions.q: What is true peak and why is it different from peak?
questions.short: True peak measures between samples, where the real waveform goes higher than any sample shows.
steps: Use a true-peak meter, not the DAW's sample-peak meter, on the master.
Target −1 dBTP for streaming delivery.
Expect lossy encoding to add up to 1 dB — that is what the margin is for.
If your sample peak reads −0.1 and true peak reads +0.4, you will clip on playback.
questions.why: Digital audio stores points, not a continuous wave; the converter reconstructs the curve between them, and that curve can exceed the highest stored sample. Encoding to MP3 or AAC shifts the waveform further, which is why platforms specify true peak rather than sample peak.
questions.watch: Mastering to −0.1 dBFS is the single most common cause of distortion that only appears on Spotify.

questions.q: Why does my master get turned down on Spotify?
questions.short: Every platform plays everything at roughly the same loudness, so a louder master just loses dynamics.
steps: Measure your integrated LUFS. If it is above −14, the platform will turn it down.
Compare your track to a reference at matched loudness, not matched fader.
Target −14 LUFS and spend the effort on balance instead of level.
If you need a loud version for clubs or DJ use, bounce that separately.
questions.why: Normalisation measures a track's loudness and applies a fixed gain so it plays at the same perceived level as everything else. A master crushed to −6 LUFS is turned down by 8 dB and arrives at the listener quieter in dynamics but identical in volume — all cost, no benefit.
questions.watch: Some platforms only turn loud tracks down and never turn quiet ones up, so a very quiet master stays quiet.

questions.q: Do I need to dither, and when?
questions.short: Only on the final bounce, only when reducing bit depth, and only once.
steps: Dither when exporting to 16-bit, typically for CD or a 16-bit WAV delivery.
Do not dither when exporting 24-bit or 32-bit float.
Dither once, on the very last export. Never twice in a chain.
If you are sending to a mastering engineer, do not dither at all.
questions.why: Truncating 24 bits to 16 creates correlated rounding errors that sound like a low-level crackle on fades. Dither adds a tiny amount of random noise that decorrelates the error, trading a theoretical hiss for an audible artefact.
questions.watch: Dithering twice adds the noise twice. If in doubt, leave it off and deliver 24-bit.

questions.q: What is crest factor and why should I care?
questions.short: The gap between peak and average level. It is the number behind whether a mix sounds punchy or flat.
steps: Compare peak and RMS or LUFS on the master. The difference is your crest factor.
Expect 8–12 dB on a dynamic mix, 5–7 on a loud modern one, under 5 on a crushed one.
If it is dropping as you mix, you are compressing more than you think.
Judge punch by this number, not by how loud the mix feels.
questions.why: The ear reads punch as the size of transients relative to everything around them, which is exactly what crest factor measures. A mix can get louder while getting less punchy, and this is the number that shows it happening.
questions.watch: A high crest factor is not automatically better. Some genres live at 5 dB by design.

questions.q: What does oversampling actually do?
questions.short: It stops distortion plugins folding harmonics back down into the audible band as false tones.
steps: Turn oversampling on for saturation, distortion, clippers and limiters.
Leave it off for EQ and most compressors — they generate little new content.
Use 2x while mixing and 4x or higher on the final bounce if the CPU allows.
Listen for it on bright sources; that is where aliasing is most audible.
questions.why: Distortion creates harmonics above the original signal, and any harmonic above half the sample rate has nowhere to go — it reflects back down as an inharmonic tone unrelated to the music. Oversampling raises the ceiling temporarily so those harmonics are generated and filtered before they fold.
questions.watch: Oversampling adds latency and CPU. Turning it on everywhere makes a session unplayable for no benefit.

questions.q: When should I EQ before compression and when after?
questions.short: Subtractive EQ before, tonal EQ after. Cut the problem the compressor would react to, then shape what is left.
steps: Put cuts first: remove rumble and resonances so the compressor does not trigger on them.
Put boosts after: a boost before the compressor will just be compressed away.
High-pass before the compressor on every source except kick and bass.
If a compressor is pumping on one frequency, the fix is a cut before it, not a different ratio.
questions.why: A compressor responds to the loudest thing in the signal, so anything you remove beforehand stops influencing its behaviour. Anything you add afterwards is not subject to its gain reduction, which is why a post-compressor boost stays and a pre-compressor one does not.
questions.watch: This is a default, not a law. A pre-compressor boost is exactly how you make a compressor emphasise a band on purpose.

questions.q: What does Q actually control?
questions.short: How wide the move is. Low Q is musical and broad; high Q is surgical and usually for fixing.
steps: Use Q 0.5–1.0 for tone shaping — it sounds like the instrument, not like EQ.
Use Q 3–8 for removing a resonance or a ring.
Match the Q to the problem: a single ringing note is narrow, a general dullness is wide.
If you need a high Q boost, you are probably solving the wrong problem.
questions.why: Q is the ratio of centre frequency to bandwidth, so a Q of 1 at 1 kHz affects roughly an octave while a Q of 8 affects a semitone or two. Broad moves sound like the source because they follow its whole character; narrow moves sound like processing because they remove one thing and leave its neighbours.
questions.watch: Very high Q boosts ring. They can sound fine in solo and awful on a sustained note.

questions.q: Shelf or bell — which should I use?
questions.short: Shelf for everything above or below a point, bell for one region. Air and warmth are shelves.
steps: Use a high shelf above 8 kHz for air, a low shelf below 150 Hz for weight.
Use a bell when the problem has a top and a bottom — mud, box, honk, ring.
If you find yourself using a very wide bell, a shelf is probably what you want.
Shelves sound more natural because they match how instruments actually roll off.
questions.why: Real acoustic behaviour is shelf-shaped: distance removes everything above a frequency, proximity adds everything below one. Bells correspond to resonances, which is also a real phenomenon — so choosing the right shape is really choosing which kind of real thing you are imitating or undoing.
questions.watch: A high shelf raises noise and hiss along with air. Check the quiet passages.

questions.q: When should I use a linear phase EQ?
questions.short: On parallel paths and multi-mic sources. Almost never on a single channel.
steps: Use it when EQing one of two signals that will be summed — parallel buses, multi-mic drums.
Use minimum phase everywhere else; it sounds more natural and costs no latency.
Do not use it on transient sources like kick and snare — it causes pre-ringing.
Mastering is the usual exception, where broad linear-phase moves are common.
questions.why: A normal EQ shifts phase around the frequencies it moves, which is inaudible on its own but causes cancellation when that signal is summed with an unprocessed copy. Linear phase avoids the shift at the cost of pre-ringing — energy that arrives before the transient, which has no acoustic equivalent and sounds unnatural on drums.
questions.watch: Linear phase adds significant latency. On a tracking session it will make overdubs unplayable.

questions.q: Why does cutting usually sound better than boosting?
aliases: should I cut instead of boost
questions.short: Cutting removes what was in the way; boosting raises noise, room and headroom along with the signal.
steps: When something is not audible, ask what is covering it before you boost it.
Cut the offender 2 dB rather than boosting the victim 2 dB.
Boost only when the content genuinely is not there, and then boost gently and wide.
Compensate the level after cutting so you are not judging the move by loudness.
questions.why: A boost amplifies everything at that frequency including hiss, room tone and bleed, and it costs headroom. A cut on a competing source changes the same ratio while reducing total energy. The maxim is a rule of thumb, not a law — but it is right more often than it is wrong.
questions.watch: Cutting on every source to make room for everything leaves a mix that is clean and thin.

questions.q: Should I high-pass everything?
aliases: do I need to high pass
questions.short: High-pass most things, but by ear and not at 120 Hz by default. The default is what makes mixes thin.
steps: Start the filter low and raise it until you hear the source change, then back off.
Expect 80 Hz on a lead vocal, 100–150 on guitars and keys, 200–300 on pads and percussion.
Do not high-pass the kick, the bass or the 808 beyond removing rumble at 30 Hz.
Check the full mix after, not the soloed channel — low end is cumulative.
questions.why: The advice comes from live multitrack work where every microphone picks up stage rumble, and it is genuinely useful there. On clean recordings there is often nothing below the fundamental to remove, so the filter only removes the instrument.
questions.watch: Six sources each high-passed 20 Hz too high adds up to a mix with no weight and no obvious culprit.

questions.q: How do I find a resonance?
questions.short: Boost narrow, sweep slowly, find what hurts, then cut it by half what you boosted.
steps: Set a bell to +8 dB with a Q of 6–8.
Sweep slowly across the suspect range while the part plays in context.
The resonance is the spot that jumps out unpleasantly, not just loudly.
Return the gain to zero, then cut 3–5 dB at that frequency.
Re-check with the boost removed — the cut is usually smaller than you expect.
questions.why: A resonance is a narrow frequency band where energy accumulates, usually from an instrument's body or a room mode. A narrow boost exaggerates it enough to locate, but the ear finds anything boosted by 8 dB objectionable, which is why the cut that follows should always be much smaller.
questions.watch: Sweeping in solo finds resonances that are inaudible in the mix. Always sweep in context.

questions.q: What is dynamic EQ and when do I need it?
questions.short: An EQ band that only engages when the signal exceeds a threshold. For problems that come and go.
steps: Use it when a frequency is only a problem sometimes — harsh on loud notes, fine on quiet ones.
Set the band first as a static cut to find the frequency, then make it dynamic.
Use a fast attack and a 60–150 ms release for musical results.
Aim for 3–5 dB of movement. More than that and something earlier in the chain is wrong.
questions.why: A static cut solves the loud moments and dulls the quiet ones. Dynamic EQ applies the cut only while the problem is present, so the source keeps its full tone everywhere else — which is exactly the behaviour you want for resonances that move with performance intensity.
questions.watch: Dynamic EQ is easy to overuse. If five bands are moving, the source needs a different treatment.

questions.q: How do I use mid/side EQ?
questions.short: Cut lows from the sides and cut presence from the mid. Small moves — 1 to 2 dB.
steps: High-pass the side channel at 120–300 Hz to keep the low end centred and mono-safe.
Cut 1–2 dB at 2–4 kHz on the mid to open space for the vocal.
Add 1 dB of air to the sides only, for width without brightening the centre.
Check mono after every move — mid/side problems are invisible in stereo.
questions.why: Mid/side separates what the two channels share from what differs between them, so you can treat the centre and the width independently. Because the sides are a difference signal, changes there are invisible in mono and can cancel audibly when summed.
questions.watch: Large mid/side moves on a mix bus are a classic way to make a record that only works on headphones.

questions.q: Which frequencies are mud, boxiness, honk and harshness?
questions.short: Mud 200–400, box 300–600, honk 800 Hz–1.5 kHz, harsh 2–5 kHz, sibilance 5–10 kHz.
steps: Mud: 200–400 Hz. Cumulative across sources, rarely one channel's fault.
Boxiness: 300–600 Hz. Usually a shell resonance or a small room.
Honk or nasal: 800 Hz–1.5 kHz. Often a horn or a mic too close and on-axis.
Harshness: 2–5 kHz. Where the ear is most sensitive, so small excesses hurt.
Sibilance: 5–10 kHz, higher for women's voices than men's.
questions.why: These bands are not arbitrary: they correspond to instrument body resonances, small-room modes and the ear's own sensitivity curve. Knowing them turns a vague complaint into a place to start sweeping, which is all a chart like this should be used for.
questions.watch: A chart is a starting point for a sweep, never a substitute for one. Every source sits slightly differently.

questions.q: How do I EQ in context instead of in solo?
questions.short: Solo to find the frequency, then unsolo to decide the amount. Never both in solo.
steps: Use solo only to locate a resonance or identify a noise.
Make every gain decision with the full mix playing.
A/B the bypass in context, not soloed — the difference is often the opposite.
If a move sounds great soloed and does nothing in the mix, undo it.
questions.why: A source in solo is competing with nothing, so the move that makes it sound best alone is usually the move that makes it fight hardest in the mix. Every useful EQ decision is about the relationship between sources, and solo removes exactly that information.
questions.watch: Some things genuinely need solo: finding a click, a noise, or a resonance. Locating is fine, deciding is not.

questions.q: Why does the same EQ move sound different on every source?
aliases: why doesnt the same eq work
questions.short: Because EQ only changes what is already there, and no two sources have the same content at that frequency.
steps: Check what is actually at the frequency before boosting it — use an analyser.
Expect the same +3 dB at 5 kHz to be air on a vocal and noise on a bass.
Use presets as a starting point for the shape, never for the gain.
Re-sweep for each source rather than copying a band position across channels.
questions.why: An equaliser is a gain control that applies to one band, so the result depends entirely on the source's content in that band. A preset encodes an assumption about the source it was made for, and that assumption is the part that does not transfer.
questions.watch: This is also why plugin presets named after famous records rarely help. They encode a different recording.

questions.q: How do I read an EQ curve?
aliases: what does the eq curve mean
questions.short: Left is low, right is high, and the axis is logarithmic — so half the width is below 600 Hz.
steps: Read left to right as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, spaced logarithmically, not evenly.
Note that an octave takes the same horizontal space anywhere, so 20–40 Hz is as wide as 10–20 kHz.
Read the vertical axis in decibels; most displays span ±12 or ±18.
Expect a filter to look enormous and a bell to look small — a filter is 18 dB, a bell is 3.
questions.why: The axis is logarithmic because pitch perception is: doubling the frequency always sounds like one octave, whether from 50 to 100 Hz or 5 to 10 kHz. A linear display would put almost the entire musical range in the leftmost tenth of the screen.
questions.watch: A plugin showing an evenly spaced frequency scale is drawing it wrong, and it will mislead you.

questions.q: What does compression ratio actually do?
questions.short: How much of the signal above the threshold gets through. At 4:1, 8 dB over becomes 2 dB over.
steps: Use 2:1–3:1 for gentle levelling where you do not want to hear it working.
Use 4:1–6:1 for control where consistency matters more than transparency.
Use 10:1 and above for limiting or for a parallel channel.
Change the threshold to set how much, and the ratio to set how hard.
questions.why: Ratio describes the slope above the threshold: at 4:1 every 4 dB of input increase produces 1 dB of output increase. Threshold decides how much of the signal is subject to that slope, which is why the two controls together determine the amount of gain reduction and neither does alone.
questions.watch: A high ratio with a high threshold can be gentler than a low ratio with a low threshold.

questions.q: What does the knee control on a compressor do?
questions.short: How gradually the compression arrives. Soft knee for transparency, hard knee for control.
steps: Use a soft knee on vocals, bass and buses, where you do not want to hear it engage.
Use a hard knee on drums and for limiting, where you want it to act decisively at a point.
If a compressor sounds like it is switching on and off, soften the knee.
Many classic hardware compressors have a fixed knee — that is part of their character.
questions.why: A hard knee applies the full ratio the instant the signal crosses the threshold, so the transition is abrupt and audible on material that hovers near it. A soft knee eases the ratio in over a range, which smooths that transition at the cost of some predictability.
questions.watch: A soft knee starts compressing below the threshold, so the meter reads gain reduction earlier than you expect.

questions.q: How do I set compressor attack by ear?
questions.short: Start slow and speed up until the transient stops poking out, then go one step slower.
steps: Start at 30 ms with the ratio and threshold already set for 4–6 dB.
Speed up gradually and listen to the attack of the source, not its level.
Stop when the transient is controlled, then back off one step to let it breathe.
On drums, too fast kills the hit; on vocals, too slow lets consonants through.
questions.why: Attack sets how long the compressor waits before reaching full gain reduction, so it decides which part of the sound is compressed and which passes untouched. On a percussive source the first few milliseconds are the entire character, which is why attack is the most consequential control on the box.
questions.watch: Attack times on different plugins are not comparable. 10 ms on one can behave like 3 ms on another.

questions.q: How do I set compressor release by ear?
questions.short: Watch the meter: it should return to zero just before the next hit. Then set it by feel.
steps: Set it so the gain reduction meter recovers fully before the next transient.
On rhythmic material, time it to the tempo — one eighth or one quarter note.
If it pumps, the release is too slow. If it sounds grainy, it is too fast.
On a bus, a slightly slow release that breathes with the tempo is often the goal.
questions.why: Release determines whether each hit starts from the same gain as the last. If the compressor has not recovered, every hit is compressed by a different amount, and that variation in time with the music is what the ear calls pumping.
questions.watch: Very fast releases on bass and low-frequency sources cause distortion, because the gain changes within a single cycle.

questions.q: What is auto-release and should I trust it?
questions.short: The compressor chooses its own release from the material. Useful on buses, lazy on sources.
steps: Use it on a mix bus or drum bus, where the material varies and a fixed release will not fit all of it.
Set it manually on individual sources, where you know what you want.
If auto-release is fixing pumping, find out why it was pumping first.
Try both and keep whichever you can defend.
questions.why: Auto-release uses two time constants — fast for transients, slow for sustained level — so it adapts to varied material better than any single setting. On a single source, where the material is consistent, that adaptation is solving a problem that does not exist and takes the decision away from you.
questions.watch: Auto-release hides pumping rather than curing it, so the underlying cause stays in the mix.

questions.q: How much gain reduction is too much?
questions.short: It depends entirely on the source: 2 dB on a mix bus, 10 dB on a rap vocal, both correct.
steps: Mix bus: 1–3 dB. Any more and you are shaping, not gluing.
Drum bus: 2–4 dB. Lead vocal: 3–6 dB. Bass: 5–8 dB. Rap vocal: 6–10 dB.
If you need more than the range for that source, split it across two compressors.
Judge by whether you can hear it working, not by the number.
questions.why: Gain reduction is only meaningful relative to how dynamic the source was. A bass guitar varying 20 dB needs 8 dB of control to be usable; a mix bus varying 6 dB needs one or two. The question is always how consistent the source needs to be, not how many decibels is respectable.
questions.watch: Two compressors doing 3 dB each sound smoother than one doing 6, on almost every source.

questions.q: Why would I use two compressors in a row?
questions.short: Each does less work, so neither becomes audible. Split the job by speed.
steps: First compressor slow: 3:1, 20–30 ms attack, 3 dB — shapes the overall level.
Second compressor fast: 4:1, 2–5 ms attack, 3 dB — catches peaks the first one let through.
Keep each one under 4 dB of gain reduction.
Use different types if you have them: opto into FET is the classic vocal pairing.
questions.why: Audibility of compression rises sharply with the amount any one unit does, so two stages of 3 dB reach the same 6 dB of control while each stays below the point where you notice it. Splitting by speed also means each one only handles the kind of dynamic it is suited to.
questions.watch: Two fast compressors in series will destroy transients even at low gain reduction. Keep the first one slow.

questions.q: What is upward compression?
questions.short: It raises what is below the threshold instead of lowering what is above it. Detail without squashing.
steps: Use it to bring up quiet detail — room tone, reverb tails, the end of a note.
Set the threshold below the average level so it acts on the quiet parts only.
Keep it to 2–4 dB; it raises noise along with the detail.
Parallel compression achieves something similar and is more widely available.
questions.why: Downward compression lowers peaks and then you make up the gain, which raises the noise floor as a side effect. Upward compression raises only the quiet material directly, leaving the peaks exactly where they were — so the transients survive untouched.
questions.watch: It raises everything quiet, including hum, hiss and headphone bleed. Clean the source first.

questions.q: VCA, FET, opto or vari-mu — which do I use when?
questions.short: VCA for control, FET for attitude, opto for smoothness, vari-mu for glue.
steps: VCA: precise and fast, with full control. Drums, bass, mix bus.
FET: very fast, adds colour. Rock vocals, rap vocals, parallel drums.
Opto: slow and program-dependent, inherently smooth. Sung vocals, bass.
Vari-mu: gentle and gets softer as it works harder. Mix bus and mastering.
questions.why: Each topology detects and reduces gain by a different physical mechanism, which gives each a characteristic attack behaviour and distortion profile. An opto cell physically cannot respond quickly, which is why it sounds smooth — the character is a consequence of the circuit, not a design choice laid on top.
questions.watch: Plugin emulations vary enormously in how faithfully they model this. Trust your ears over the name.

questions.q: How is a limiter different from a compressor?
questions.short: A limiter is a compressor with a very high ratio and a near-instant attack. It stops peaks, it does not shape.
steps: Use a compressor to shape dynamics and a limiter to catch what escapes.
Put the limiter last, after everything that could add level.
Aim for 2–4 dB of limiting on a master; more is a balance problem.
Use true-peak limiting for anything going to streaming.
questions.why: There is no categorical difference — a limiter is a compressor set so steeply that nothing meaningfully exceeds the threshold. The distinction is in intent: a compressor changes how the material feels, a limiter guarantees a ceiling.
questions.watch: Limiters applied to shape rather than protect produce flat, lifeless masters very quickly.

questions.q: What is multiband compression actually for?
questions.short: Controlling one frequency range independently. Usually a sign the mix needs fixing instead.
steps: Use it when one band is genuinely dynamic — a boomy low end, a harsh top on some notes.
Use two or three bands, never five.
Keep the crossover points away from the fundamental of anything important.
Ask first whether dynamic EQ or fixing the source would do the same job more simply.
questions.why: Multiband splits the signal, compresses each part separately and recombines, which gives frequency-selective control that full-band compression cannot. The cost is phase interaction at the crossovers and a tendency to flatten the natural relationship between bands.
questions.watch: Multiband on a mix bus is usually patching a problem that one channel caused. Find that channel.

questions.q: When is a transient shaper better than a compressor?
questions.short: When you want more attack rather than less dynamic range. It ignores level entirely.
steps: Use it when a quiet hit and a loud hit both need more attack.
Raise attack for definition, lower sustain for tightness.
Use it before the compressor, so the compressor responds to the shaped signal.
Keep moves modest: +3 to +6 on attack is usually plenty.
questions.why: A compressor is level-dependent, so it treats a quiet hit differently from a loud one. A transient shaper detects the shape of the envelope regardless of level, which is why it can add attack to every hit equally where a compressor can only add it to the ones above threshold.
questions.watch: Transient shapers raise bleed and room along with the attack. On live kits, gate first.

questions.q: Why does my compressor make things quieter and duller?
questions.short: You are compressing the transients, which carry most of the high frequency content.
steps: Slow the attack so the transient passes before gain reduction starts.
Make up the gain properly; a lot of perceived dullness is just lower level.
Try a cleaner compressor type — some emulations roll off the top as part of their character.
Put a high shelf after the compressor rather than before it.
questions.why: A transient contains a burst of high-frequency energy, so clamping it with a fast attack removes treble as a side effect of removing level. The compressor is not filtering anything — it is just that the brightest part of the sound was also the loudest.
questions.watch: Comparing at different levels always makes the quieter one sound duller. Match gain before judging.

questions.q: What is lookahead?
questions.short: The processor delays the audio so it can see a peak coming and act before it arrives.
steps: Use it on limiters so peaks are caught without needing a zero-length attack.
Use a few milliseconds; more than 5 ms starts to sound unnatural on transients.
Expect latency equal to the lookahead time — the DAW compensates on playback, not while tracking.
Turn it off when tracking or monitoring through the plugin.
questions.why: A detector cannot react to a transient faster than the transient itself. Delaying the audio path by a few milliseconds lets the detector analyse the signal before the listener hears it, so gain reduction can be fully in place at the instant the peak arrives.
questions.watch: Long lookahead on a limiter can audibly duck the material just before a loud hit.

questions.q: What does the sidechain filter on a compressor do?
questions.short: It stops the compressor reacting to frequencies you do not want it to follow. Usually the kick.
steps: High-pass the sidechain at 80–120 Hz on any bus compressor.
On a vocal, high-pass the detector so plosives stop triggering the whole chain.
Use it before changing ratio or threshold when something pumps.
Listen to the sidechain signal if the plugin lets you — it tells you what it is reacting to.
questions.why: A compressor responds to total energy, and low frequencies contain far more energy than anything else. Without a filter, a bus compressor is effectively a kick-triggered ducker — filtering the detector lets it respond to the music instead.
questions.watch: Filtering the sidechain does not filter the audio. The low end still gets compressed, just not by itself.

questions.q: What is bus compression for?
questions.short: Making several sources move as one. It is about shared behaviour, not level control.
steps: Use 2:1 or 3:1 with a slow attack and 2–4 dB of gain reduction.
High-pass the sidechain so the low end stops driving it.
Set the release to the tempo so the bus breathes with the song.
Put it in early and mix into it, rather than adding it at the end.
questions.why: When one compressor controls several sources, every source ducks when any one of them is loud. That shared gain movement is the cue the ear uses to decide that sounds belong together, which is why glue is a real effect and not just a word.
questions.watch: Adding bus compression at the end changes every balance decision you made underneath it.

questions.q: How do I compress without losing dynamics?
questions.short: Compress the small variations and automate the big ones. They are different problems.
steps: Automate section-level changes with the fader — verse to chorus is not a compressor's job.
Let the compressor handle variation within a phrase only.
Use parallel compression so the uncompressed signal keeps its peaks.
Keep any single compressor under 4 dB and use two if you need more.
questions.why: Musical dynamics are a structural property — the chorus is bigger than the verse — while the dynamics a compressor fixes are moment-to-moment inconsistencies. Using a compressor to flatten both destroys the first in order to fix the second.
questions.watch: If the compressor is working hard in the chorus and barely in the verse, that is automation's job.

questions.q: What is an expander and when do I use one?
questions.short: A gentle gate. It lowers quiet material by a ratio instead of silencing it.
steps: Use it to reduce bleed and room tone without the abruptness of a gate.
Set a ratio of 1:1.5 or 1:2 and expect 3–8 dB of reduction in the gaps.
Use it on toms and live drums where a gate sounds obvious.
Set the threshold just below the quietest wanted hit.
questions.why: A gate is an expander with an extreme ratio, so the only difference is how completely the quiet material is removed. Keeping some of it preserves the sense of a real room, which is often the thing that made the recording worth keeping.
questions.watch: Expanders on sustained sources chatter on the decay. Lengthen the hold time.

questions.q: How do I set a gate properly?
questions.short: Set the range first, not the threshold. 10–15 dB of reduction beats silence on almost everything.
steps: Set range or depth to 10–15 dB so the gate reduces rather than mutes.
Set the threshold just under the quietest hit you want to keep.
Fast attack, 10–50 ms hold, 100–300 ms release so the decay is not chopped.
Key the gate from a filtered version of the source if it triggers on bleed.
questions.why: A gate that closes completely creates silence between hits, and silence is unnatural on any instrument recorded in a room. Reducing rather than muting keeps the room continuous while removing enough bleed to regain control.
questions.watch: Setting the threshold with the part soloed almost always leaves it triggering wrongly in the mix.

questions.q: What is ducking and when should I use it?
questions.short: Using one source to lower another automatically. For anything that competes only some of the time.
steps: Side-chain the quieter-serving source to the one that must win — pads to vocal, music to speech.
Use 2–4 dB with a slow 200–300 ms release so it is felt, not heard.
Duck the reverb returns under the dry vocal; it clears more space than ducking the source.
Check with the trigger muted that the ducked source still sounds correct.
questions.why: A static balance has to serve both the moments when two sources overlap and the moments when they do not, and no single level does both. Ducking makes the balance time-varying so each source can be loud exactly when nothing is competing with it.
questions.watch: Fast ducking on sustained material is audible as pumping. The release is the setting that matters.

questions.q: How do I sidechain without the whole mix pumping?
questions.short: Duck less, release faster, and only duck the band that is actually in the way.
steps: Reduce the amount to 2–3 dB. Most audible pumping is simply too much.
Shorten the release so it recovers before the next beat.
Use a frequency-selective ducker so only the clashing band moves.
Duck the sub only, not the whole source, when the clash is with a kick.
questions.why: Pumping is audible when the gain change is large, slow, or applied to frequencies that did not need it. Each of those is a separate dial, which is why reducing the amount alone often does not fix it.
questions.watch: In some genres the pump is the production. Decide whether you are removing a fault or a feature.

questions.q: How do I set reverb decay to the tempo?
questions.short: The tail should end before the next chord change. One bar is the usual answer.
steps: Work out one bar in seconds: 240 divided by the BPM in 4/4.
Start with a decay of about one bar and shorten until the tail stops smearing chord changes.
At fast tempos use half a bar; at ballad tempos one to two bars.
Check on the busiest section, not the sparsest.
questions.why: Reverb that is still sounding when the harmony changes overlays two chords, which the ear hears as mud rather than as space. Tying decay to the bar makes the tail a musical length instead of an arbitrary one, so it resolves with the music.
questions.watch: The PulseRoom Reverb page calculates these from your project tempo — use it rather than doing the arithmetic.

questions.q: Room, plate, hall, chamber or spring — which when?
questions.short: Room for glue, plate for vocals, hall for size, chamber for warmth, spring for character.
steps: Room, 0.4–1.2 s: puts sources in a shared space. Drums, guitars, glue.
Plate, 1.0–2.5 s: dense and bright with no early reflections. The classic vocal reverb.
Hall, 1.8–3.5 s: large and slow. Choirs, strings, ballads.
Chamber, 1.0–2.0 s: warm and smooth. Vocals and horns.
Spring: coloured and twangy. Guitars, dub, and anywhere you want it heard.
questions.why: The types differ mainly in how quickly the reflections become dense and how the high end decays. A plate has no early reflections at all, which is why it adds size without placing a voice in a specific room — the reason it has been the default vocal reverb for sixty years.
questions.watch: Using four different reverbs in one mix puts every source in a different building.

questions.q: What are early reflections and why do they matter?
questions.short: The first few bounces off nearby surfaces. They tell the ear how big the room is and how close you are.
steps: Raise early reflections to place a source in a specific room.
Lower them, or use a plate, to add size without a sense of place.
Use them instead of level to push a source back — they read as distance.
Keep them short, under 40 ms, or they become audible as separate echoes.
questions.why: The brain locates sources by comparing the direct sound with the first reflections — their delay tells it how far the walls are, their level how far away the source is. The diffuse tail that follows carries much less positional information, which is why early reflections are the part that creates realism.
questions.watch: Strong early reflections on a lead vocal make it sound recorded in a bad room, which is rarely the goal.

questions.q: Should reverb go on a send or an insert?
questions.short: Send, nearly always. It lets several sources share one space and lets you EQ the tail separately.
steps: Set up two or three reverb sends for the whole mix, not one per channel.
Set the reverb to 100% wet on the send.
EQ the return: high-pass at 300 Hz, low-pass around 8 kHz.
Use an insert only when the effect is part of the sound, like a spring on a guitar.
questions.why: Sources in one shared reverb sound like they are in one room, which is most of what makes a mix cohere. A send also separates the wet signal so you can filter and compress the tail without touching the dry source.
questions.watch: Leaving the reverb at less than 100% wet on a send mixes the dry signal in twice and shifts the balance.

questions.q: How do I EQ a reverb return?
questions.short: High-pass at 300 Hz and low-pass around 8 kHz. More aggressively than feels right.
steps: High-pass the return at 250–400 Hz. Low end in a tail is pure mud.
Low-pass at 7–10 kHz so the tail does not add hiss and sibilance.
Cut the same resonance you cut on the source, or it comes back in the tail.
De-ess the send if the reverb is spitting on consonants.
questions.why: A reverb tail lasts seconds while the source lasts moments, so any frequency present in the tail is present far longer in total. Low mids that are harmless on the dry signal become continuous in the return, which is why reverb is the most common hidden cause of a muddy mix.
questions.watch: Filtering the return too hard makes the reverb sound like a telephone in the distance.

questions.q: How do I use delay instead of reverb for depth?
questions.short: A short delay places a source back without the wash. It keeps the mix clean where reverb clouds it.
steps: Use a single repeat at 60–140 ms, low in the mix, with no feedback.
Filter it: high-pass at 400 Hz and low-pass at 5 kHz so it sits behind.
Pan it slightly off the source, or use a stereo delay with different times per side.
Add reverb to the delay return rather than to the source.
questions.why: Depth cues are mostly time-based: a reflection arriving late tells the ear the source is far from a surface. A single filtered repeat supplies that cue with a fraction of the energy a reverb adds, so it costs almost nothing in clarity.
questions.watch: A slap delay on a fast vocal can blur the words. Shorten it or lower the level.

questions.q: What is pre-delay and how do I set it?
questions.short: The gap before the reverb starts. It keeps words clear while the space stays big.
steps: Set it to a 1/64 or 1/32 note at your tempo — typically 20–45 ms.
Longer pre-delay keeps the source upfront; zero fuses it into the room and pushes it back.
On a fast song use a shorter pre-delay so the tail does not land on the next word.
Use the PulseRoom Reverb page to get the note value at your project tempo.
questions.why: The ear fuses sounds arriving within about 30 ms of each other into one event, so reverb starting immediately is heard as part of the voice and makes it distant. A gap lets the dry consonants arrive alone before the room responds, which is why a wet vocal can still be intelligible.
questions.watch: Beyond about 60 ms the pre-delay stops being a gap and starts being an audible echo.

questions.q: What is frequency masking?
aliases: why cant I hear it in the mix
questions.short: A loud sound makes a quieter one at a nearby frequency inaudible, even though both are playing.
steps: When something is buried, find what else occupies its range before you raise it.
Cut the competitor 2 dB rather than boosting the victim 2 dB.
Separate by pitch, by time or by stereo position, not just by level.
Check by muting the suspected masker — if the buried source appears, you found it.
questions.why: The ear analyses sound in overlapping frequency bands, and within a band the loudest component suppresses the perception of quieter ones. This is physiology, not a mixing convention — which is why raising the masked source never fully works and removing the overlap always does.
questions.watch: Masking is strongest upward: a loud low sound masks higher ones more than the reverse.

questions.q: What is the Fletcher-Munson curve and why does it matter?
aliases: why does my mix change with volume
questions.short: Your ears hear bass and treble less at low volume, so the same mix changes character with level.
steps: Mix at a consistent level, around 75–83 dB SPL, so your frequency perception stays constant.
Check quietly as well: at low level, balance problems are easier to hear than tonal ones.
If the mix only works loud, you probably added low end at low volume.
Use a reference at matched loudness, never matched fader.
questions.why: Human hearing sensitivity varies with frequency and that variation itself changes with level — the ear is relatively less sensitive to extremes when quiet. A mix balanced at 60 dB will sound bass-heavy at 90, and neither version is wrong; the monitoring level was simply inconsistent.
questions.watch: This is also why loud always sounds better. Any A/B at different levels is a rigged comparison.

questions.q: What volume should I mix at?
questions.short: Around 75–83 dB SPL for balance work, quieter for most of it, loud only in short bursts.
steps: Set one reference level with a meter or a phone app and mark the knob.
Do most of your work quieter than that; balance is easier to judge at low level.
Go loud only briefly, to check low end and excitement.
Never make tonal decisions at a level you have not calibrated.
questions.why: Because frequency perception changes with level, a consistent monitoring level is what makes your judgements repeatable from day to day. The specific number matters less than it being the same number every time.
questions.watch: Long sessions at high level cause fatigue that makes you add treble you will regret.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound worse the longer I work on it?
questions.short: Ear fatigue. Your sensitivity to high frequencies drops, so you keep adding treble that is already there.
steps: Stop every 45–60 minutes for at least ten minutes of silence.
Lower the monitoring level as the session goes on, not up.
Make the brightness decisions early, when your ears are fresh.
Sleep on it. The next morning's first listen is the most honest one you will get.
questions.why: Sustained exposure temporarily shifts hearing thresholds, most noticeably in the 2–6 kHz region. You compensate by adding exactly the frequencies you have become less sensitive to, which is why fatigued mixes are reliably too bright rather than randomly wrong.
questions.watch: If you are making bigger moves than an hour ago, you are fatigued rather than making progress.

questions.q: How do I use reference tracks properly?
questions.short: Match loudness first, use two or three, and listen for one thing at a time.
steps: Match the reference's loudness to your mix, by ear or with a meter. Never compare at different levels.
Use two or three references, not one, so you are not copying one engineer's taste.
Listen for one attribute per pass: low end, then vocal level, then width.
Pick references in the same genre and from the last few years.
questions.why: A commercial reference is a known-good target heard on the same speakers in the same room, which removes your monitoring from the comparison. Matching loudness first is non-negotiable, because at different levels the louder track always wins regardless of quality.
questions.watch: Referencing too early paralyses a mix. Get your own balance down first, then compare.

questions.q: How do I A/B without fooling myself?
aliases: how to compare before and after
questions.short: Match the gain before you compare. An unmatched A/B always picks the louder one.
steps: Match output level between the two states before deciding anything.
Switch quickly; the ear's memory for timbre is a few seconds at best.
Decide which is better before you know which is which, if you can.
If you cannot hear a difference at matched gain, there is no difference worth keeping.
questions.why: Louder is perceived as better across almost every attribute — fuller, clearer, more exciting — and most processing adds a little level. Without gain matching, you are not comparing the processing, you are comparing the gain.
questions.watch: Plugins with auto-gain help, but check them: most only match RMS, not perceived loudness.

questions.q: Why does louder always sound better?
aliases: why does turning it up help
questions.short: Because your ears hear more bass and treble as level rises. It is physiology, not quality.
steps: Assume any comparison where one side is louder is invalid.
Match levels with a meter before judging a plugin, a mix or a master.
Be suspicious of any processing that makes things louder as a side effect.
Turn down rather than up when deciding whether something is working.
questions.why: Equal-loudness contours flatten as level rises, so a louder playback genuinely delivers proportionally more low and high frequency to your ear. The louder version is not better, it is being heard with a different frequency response.
questions.watch: This bias is strong enough that it defeats trained engineers. Gain matching is not optional.

questions.q: How do I check a mix on different speakers?
questions.short: Phone, car, headphones, laptop. Listen for a different thing on each and fix only what recurs.
steps: Phone speaker: can you hear the bass line and the vocal? That is a mid-range test.
Car: is the low end out of control? Cars exaggerate 60–120 Hz.
Earbuds: is the stereo width comfortable and the reverb tasteful?
Laptop: is anything missing entirely?
Only fix problems that appear on two or more systems.
questions.why: Every system has its own frequency response and its own failure mode, so a problem on one is as likely to be that speaker as your mix. A problem on two or more is yours.
questions.watch: Chasing every system in turn produces a mix that is a compromise of everything and good on nothing.

questions.q: What is a null test and what does it prove?
questions.short: Invert one of two signals and sum them. Silence means they are identical.
steps: Duplicate a track, invert the polarity of one copy and play both.
Perfect silence means the two are bit-identical.
Use it to check whether a plugin is actually doing anything, or whether two bounces match.
Remember a null proves identity, not quality — two signals can differ audibly and still almost null.
questions.why: Summing a signal with its exact inverse cancels completely. Anything left over is the difference between them, so the test isolates precisely what a process changed — which is far more informative than listening to the result.
questions.watch: A null test cannot compare plugins that add latency or gain. Match both first or the result is meaningless.

questions.q: How do I train my ears to recognise frequencies?
questions.short: Boost a known frequency hard on music you know, listen, then remove it. Fifteen minutes a day.
steps: Pick one frequency. Boost it 10 dB on a familiar track and listen for a minute.
Remove it, then try to hear it again without the boost.
Work through 100, 250, 500, 1k, 3k, 8k before adding anything in between.
Use a free ear-training app for blind testing once you can name the obvious ones.
Do it for fifteen minutes rather than two hours — attention matters more than duration.
questions.why: Recognising a frequency is a learned association between a sound and a number, and like any such association it forms through repeated labelled exposure. Boosting makes the label unmistakable; the skill is in then hearing it without the boost.
questions.watch: Training on pink noise transfers poorly to music. Use real tracks you know well.
